'''''Cirsium vulgare''''', commonly known as '''spear thistle''', '''bull thistle''', or '''common thistle''', is a species of the [[Asteraceae]] genus ''[[Cirsium]]'', native throughout most of Europe (north to 66°N, locally 68°N), [[Western Asia]] (east to the [[Yenisei]] Valley), and [[North Africa|northwestern Africa]] ([[Atlas Mountains]]).<ref name=FloraE>''Flora Europaea'': [http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Cirsium&SPECIES_XREF=vulgare&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= ''Cirsium vulgare'']</ref><ref>Den Virtuella Floran: [http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/astera/cirsi/cirsvul.html ''Cirsium vulgare''] (in Swedish, with maps)</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=cirsium+vulgare Altervista Flora Italiana, Cardo asinino, ''Cirsium vulgare'' (Savi) Ten.]</ref><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200023702 Flora of China, <big>翼蓟</big> yi ji, ''Cirsium vulgare'' (Savi) Tenore]</ref> It is also [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in North America, Africa, and Australia and is an [[invasive species|invasive]] weed in several regions.<ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200023702 Flora of North America, Bull or common or spear thistle, gros chardon, chardon vulgaire ou lancéolé, piqueux, ''Cirsium vulgare'' (Savi) Tenore]</ref><ref>[http://bie.ala.org.au/species/Cirsium+vulgare Atlas of Living Australia, ''Cirsium vulgare'' (Savi) Ten., Black Thistle]</ref><ref>[http://www.ville-ge.ch/musinfo/bd/cjb/africa/details.php?langue=an&id=104607 Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques & South African National Biodiversity Institute, African Plant Database, ''Cirsium vulgare'' (Savi) Ten.]</ref> It is the national flower of [[Scotland]].

The plant provides a great deal of [[nectar]] for [[pollinators]]. It was rated in the top 10 for most nectar production (nectar per unit cover per year) in a [[UK]] plants survey conducted by the AgriLand project which is supported by the UK Insect Pollinators Initiative.<ref name=Pollinators>{{cite web |title=Which flowers are the best source of nectar? |publisher=Conservation Grade |url=http://www.conservationgrade.org/2014/10/which_flowers_best_source_nectar/ |access-date=18 October 2017 |date=15 October 2014 |archive-date=14 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191214024659/http://www.conservationgrade.org/2014/10/which_flowers_best_source_nectar/ }}</ref> Marsh thistle, ''[[Cirsium palustre]]'', was ranked in first place while this thistle was ranked in sixth place. It also was a top producer of nectar sugar in another study in Britain, ranked third with a production per floral unit of (2300 ± 400 μg).<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hicks|first1=DM|last2=Ouvrard|first2=P|last3=Baldock|first3=KCR|title=Food for Pollinators: Quantifying the Nectar and Pollen Resources of Urban Flower Meadows|journal=PLOS ONE |volume=11 |issue=6|article-number=e0158117|date=2016|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0158117|pmid=27341588|pmc=4920406|bibcode=2016PLoSO..1158117H|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Description ==
It is a tall [[biennial plant|biennial]] or short-lived [[monocarpic]] [[thistle]], forming a [[rosette (botany)|rosette]] of [[leaf|leaves]] and a [[taproot]] up to 70 cm (28 in) long in the first year, and a [[flower]]ing stem 1–1.5 m (3 ft 4 in – 4 ft 11 in) tall in the second (rarely third or fourth) year. It can grow up to {{Convert|1.8|m}} tall.<ref name="Elias-2009" /> It sometimes will function as an annual, flowering in the first year. The stem is winged, with numerous longitudinal spine-tipped wings along its full length. The leaves are stoutly spined, grey-green, deeply lobed; the basal leaves grow up to {{Convert|30|cm}} long,<ref name="Elias-2009" /> with smaller leaves on the upper part of the flower stem; the leaf lobes are spear-shaped (from which the English name derives). The [[inflorescence]] is {{Convert|2.5-5|cm|0}} diameter, pink-purple, with all the [[floret]]s of similar form (no division into disc and ray florets). The [[seed]]s are {{convert|5|mm|1}} long, with a downy [[Pappus (flower structure)|pappus]], which assists in wind dispersal. As in other species of ''Cirsium'' (but unlike species in the related genus ''[[Carduus]]''), the pappus hairs are feathery with fine side hairs.<ref name=blamey>Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}</ref><ref name=Organic>Bond, W., Davies, G., & Turner, R. J. (2007). [https://www.gardenorganic.org.uk/sites/www.gardenorganic.org.uk/files/organic-weeds/cirsium-vulgare.pdf The biology and non-chemical control Spear Thistle (''Cirsium vulgare'').] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201107235925/https://www.gardenorganic.org.uk/sites/www.gardenorganic.org.uk/files/organic-weeds/cirsium-vulgare.pdf |date=7 November 2020 }} 6pp. HDRA the organic organisation. [https://web.archive.org/web/20060830211100/http://www.gardenorganic.org.uk/organicweeds/downloads/cirsium%20vulgare.pdf 2006 Version]</ref>

== Ecology ==
Spear thistle is often a [[ruderal species]], colonising bare [[disturbed ground]], but also persists well on heavily [[grazing|grazed]] land as it is unpalatable to most grazing animals.<ref name=Organic/> Nitrogen-rich soils help increase its proliferation.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cwma.org/BullThistle.html|title=Bull thistle|publisher=Colorado Weed Management Association|access-date=27 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150929010217/http://www.cwma.org/BullThistle.html|archive-date=29 September 2015}}</ref> The flowers are a rich nectar source used by numerous pollinating insects, including [[honey bee]]s, [[Anthidium manicatum|wool-carder bees]], and many [[butterfly|butterflies]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Cirsium vulgare (Savi) Ten.|url=http://florabase.calm.wa.gov.au/browse/profile/7937|work=Department of Environment and Conservation|publisher=Government of Western Australia|access-date=7 July 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110322180027/http://florabase.calm.wa.gov.au/browse/profile/7937|archive-date=22 March 2011}}</ref> The seeds are eaten by [[European goldfinch|goldfinches]], [[linnet]]s and [[European greenfinch|greenfinches]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Spear thistle – Cirsium vulgare|url=http://www.plantpress.com/wildlife/o799-spearthistle.php|work=Natural England|publisher=The Plant Press|access-date=7 July 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110929085200/http://www.plantpress.com/wildlife/o799-spearthistle.php|archive-date=29 September 2011}}</ref> The seeds are dispersed by wind, mud, water, and possibly also by [[ant]]s; they do not show significant long-term dormancy, most germinating soon after dispersal and only a few lasting up to four years in the [[soil seed bank]].<ref name=weedaus>{{cite web|title=Spear thistle|url=http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&state=&s=&ibra=all&card=H71|work=Weed Australia|publisher=Australian Weeds Committee National Initiative|access-date=7 July 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927171539/http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&state=&s=&ibra=all&card=H71|archive-date=27 September 2011}}</ref> Seed is also often spread by human activity such as [[hay]] bales.<ref name=Organic/>

=== Weed status ===
Spear thistle is designated an "injurious weed" under the UK [[Weeds Act 1959]],<ref>Defra, UK – Farming – Wildlife and plants [http://www.defra.gov.uk/farm/wildlife/weeds/index.htm Ragwort and injurious weeds] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070430174831/http://www.defra.gov.uk/farm/wildlife/weeds/index.htm |date=30 April 2007 }}</ref> and a [[noxious weed]] in Australia<ref name=weedaus/><ref>{{cite web|title=Spear Thistle|url=http://www.dpi.vic.gov.au/dpi/vro/vrosite.nsf/pages/sip_spear_thistle|work=Department of Primary Industries|publisher=Victorian Government|access-date=7 July 2011}}</ref><ref name=PIRSA>{{cite web|title=Declared Plant Policy|url=http://www.pir.sa.gov.au/_media/pdf/pirsa_internet/biosecurity/nrm_biosecurity/pest_weed_policies/declared_plants_2/spear_thistle_policy.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110315061128/http://www.pir.sa.gov.au/_media/pdf/pirsa_internet/biosecurity/nrm_biosecurity/pest_weed_policies/declared_plants_2/spear_thistle_policy.pdf|archive-date=15 March 2011|work=Primary Industries and Resources SA|publisher=Government of South Australia|access-date=7 July 2011}}</ref> and in nine US states.<ref name="USDA">{{cite web |title=USDA Plants Profile for ''Cirsium vulgare'' |url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=CIVU |access-date=5 August 2024 |work=USDA Plant Database |publisher=USDA}}</ref> Spread is only by seed, not by root fragments as in the related [[Cirsium arvense|creeping thistle]] ''C. arvense''. It is best cleared from land by hoeing and deep cutting of the taproot before seeds mature; regular cultivation also prevents its establishment.<ref name=Organic/>

Despite this label, the plant has beneficial qualities beyond its very high [[nectar]] production. It produces seeds eaten by the [[American goldfinch]], down from seed pods that is used by those birds for [[nest]]ing material. However, despite this serving [[Generalist species|generalist]] pollinators and animals, in America it is highly recommended to plant [[Native species|native]] thistles and other plants as it can wreak havoc on natural ecosystems.

== Other names ==
Common names include '''bull thistle''',<ref name=Organic/><ref name=USDA2>{{GRIN | access-date = 15 December 2017}}</ref> '''Scots''', '''Scottish''', or '''Scotch thistle''', and '''common thistle'''.<ref name=USDA2/>

== Uses ==
The stems can be peeled (removing their spiny surfaces) and then steamed or boiled.<ref name="Elias-2009">{{cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|page=115|oclc=244766414|orig-date=1982}}</ref> They are often pickled in cajun cuisine.{{citation needed|date=March 2026}} The tap roots can be eaten raw or cooked, but are only palatable on young thistles that have not yet flowered.<ref>{{cite web |title=Cirsium |url=http://www.survival.org.au/bf_cirsium.php |work=Survival and Self Sufficiency |access-date=9 September 2011}}</ref> The dried florets steeped in water are used in rural Italy for curdling goats' milk in preparation for making cheese.{{citation needed|date=November 2020}} In Iran, cleaned stems are used in the dish Khoresh-e-Kangar (thistle stem stew).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Daryabandari |first=Najaf |title=از سیر تا پیاز آشپزی |isbn=978-964-431-012-6}}</ref>

== In culture ==
The plant features in some Scottish ceremonies such as the "Riding of the Marches", held annually in [[Langholm]] in July. The 1992 specimen measured six feet in length.<ref name = "Mabey">Mabey R. (1996). ''Flora Britannica''. Sinclair-Stevenson. {{ISBN|1-85619-377-2}}.</ref>

Spear thistle is also the emblem of [[Newton Regis]] in England.<ref name= "Mabey" />
